 Linus Uhlig Sat, 31 October 2026 at 5:04 am GMT-5 3 min read A worker on the minimum wage will earn more than half the salary needed to trigger the higher rate of tax from April, figures show. 
 At the turn of the century, the higher-rate tax threshold was nearly five times the minimum wage, according to analysis from insurer IG. 
 But this ratio will fall to less than two times in 2026-27 after years of income tax thresholds failing to keep pace with a soaring minimum wage. 
 At his maiden Budget on Wednesday, John Healey, the Chancellor, announced that the minimum hourly rate paid to workers aged 21 or older would rise by 3.9pc to £13.21 from next April. 
 The 50p increase will take annual living wage earnings to above £25,700, assuming a standard 37.5-hour working week – more than half of the £50,270 higher-rate tax threshold. 
 By contrast, income tax thresholds have been frozen since 2021-22 and will remain as such until at least 2030-31. 
 The figures highlight growing wage compression, as low-paid workers close the gap on traditionally more skilled middle-earners . 
 Gareth Davies, the shadow financial secretary to the Treasury, said: "Labour is using every means at its disposal to squeeze Middle England dry. Our country is on course for the highest tax burden in history." 
 When the minimum wage was first introduced in 1999, the higher-rate tax threshold was 4.6 times higher than the annual minimum wage rate . Since then, the threshold has increased by just 56pc while the minimum wage has grown by 266pc. 
 Valentin Boboc, a senior economist at the Institute of Economic Affairs think tank, said: "Being a higher-rate taxpayer is certainly not a sign of affluence any more. The Budget has extended the freeze on tax thresholds until 2031, prolonging the squeeze on middle earners." 
 Michael Healy, the chief executive of IG Consumer, said: "What was once a tax reserved for relatively high earners is increasingly catching ordinary working households. 
 "Twenty-five years ago, someone needed to earn more than four times the minimum wage before paying higher-rate income tax. Today, that figure is barely twice the minimum wage, and by next year it is projected to fall below that level for the first time." 
 Since 2023, almost two million more taxpayers have been dragged into paying higher tax rates. HMRC said the number of higher-rate taxpayers is projected to reach 7.7 million for the 2026-27 tax year, an increase of 33.8pc from 2023-24. 
 This fiscal drag means that 18.9pc of taxpayers will qualify for the higher-rate tax next year. 
 David Little, of wealth manager Evelyn Partners, said: "The narrowing gap between the minimum wage and the higher-rate income tax threshold is a striking illustration of how the UK's tax system has failed to keep pace with wage growth." 
 Story continues The Treasury confirmed that the Government had set out its approach to income tax until April 2031 and that it was making targeted choices on tax.
